screens.title: WLC Initial Setup
screens.narratorSegment: Initial setup of a Wireless LAN Controller is the moment you establish control, security, and reachability for your wireless domain. A WLC needs a management IP, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS so administrators can access it from the network. You will also create administrative credentials. These basic settings are not optional: if the management IP is incorrect or the gateway is missing, APs and administrators may not reach the controller. Configure DNS so the WLC can resolve names during some discovery workflows. Immediately change default passwords and restrict which management hosts can access the controller to reduce risk. A concrete example: assign the WLC management interface 192.168.1.10/24 with gateway 192.168.1.1 and DNS 192.168.1.2, then create an admin account with a strong passphrase. A common misconception is that APs can always register without the management plane secured — they may join technically, but unsecured management credentials leave the whole deployment vulnerable. Key takeaway: the management plane is the root of trust for controller-based Wi‑Fi. Verify connectivity with a browser to the default management IP or a console session and confirm you can reach the WLC from your management workstation. What access controls will you put in place for your controller?

keyIdea.text: Set a reachable management IP, configure DNS/gateway, and secure admin credentials before creating WLANs.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › WLC Initial Setup
Definition
The WLC initial setup configures the controller’s management interface and administrative access so it can manage APs and WLANs.
Required settings
  • Management IP, subnet mask, default gateway
  • DNS servers for name resolution
  • Administrative credentials and access restrictions
Concrete Example
Assign management IP 192.168.1.10/24, gateway 192.168.1.1, DNS 192.168.1.2, then create an admin account with a strong passphrase.
Common Mistake
Leaving default passwords and wide management access opens the controller to unauthorized changes. Always restrict management IPs.
Key Takeaway

Secure and reachable management settings are required before deploying WLANs or allowing APs to join.

Quick Setup Steps
  1. Connect to console or default management IP via browser.
  2. Set management IP, mask, gateway, and DNS on the WLC interface.
  3. Create administrative user and change default password.
  4. Limit management access to specific subnets or IPs.
  5. Verify reachability from your admin workstation.
Why it matters
The management plane is the single point from which WLANs and APs are configured. If it is misconfigured or compromised, the entire wireless fabric is affected.

screens.title: Creating WLANs and SSIDs
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a WLAN on a WLC means defining a profile the controller uses to broadcast an SSID to clients and to apply security and network mapping. The process begins by choosing a profile name for internal reference and an SSID that users will see. You then enable the WLAN and select security settings. For example, choose the WPA2 policy and enable AES to use CCMP encryption. In the controller GUI the path is typically WLANs → Create New; in the CLI you create the WLAN ID, give it a name, enable it, and attach security settings. An example CLI sequence creates WLAN ID 2 with SSID MyCorpNet, enables it, configures WPA2-PSK and AES, and maps it to a VLAN interface named vlan20. A common misconception is that SSID broadcasting alone controls access; in reality, security policy and VLAN mapping determine authentication and network reachability. Key takeaway: a WLAN is a bundle of SSID, security policy, and network interface mapping — all three must be correct for users to connect and get an IP on the intended subnet. How would you document your WLAN naming and VLAN strategy for a multi-SSID deployment?

keyIdea.title: WLAN = SSID + Security + VLAN
keyIdea.text: Each WLAN definition ties a broadcast SSID to a security policy and a logical interface so clients authenticate and receive the correct network access.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Creating WLANs and SSIDs
Step-by-step
Define profile name, SSID, security, and VLAN mapping.
GUI path (typical)
WLANs → Create New → Profile Name → SSID → Security → Interface/VLAN mapping → Enable
Security selection
Choose WPA2, enable AES (CCMP). For small deployments choose PSK; for enterprises choose 802.1X with RADIUS.
VLAN mapping
Assign the WLAN to a dynamic interface that represents the VLAN so clients get IPs from the correct subnet.
Key Takeaway

SSIDs are UI-facing names; the WLAN profile ties that name to security and a logical interface for real network access.

Concrete CLI Example
! Create a new WLAN (SSID)
(WLC)> config wlan create 2 MyCorpNet MyCorpNet
(WLC)> config wlan description 2 "Employee Network"
(WLC)> config wlan enable 2

! Configure WPA2-Personal (PSK) security for WLAN ID 2
(WLC)> config wlan security wpa wpa2 enable 2
(WLC)> config wlan security wpa wpa2 ciphers aes enable 2
(WLC)> config wlan security wpa wpa2 psk set-key ascii CohortiaWLAN!23 2

! Map WLAN ID 2 to dynamic interface vlan20
(WLC)> config wlan interface 2 vlan20
Misconception
Broadcasting an SSID does not automatically provide access; the security policy and correct VLAN interface determine whether a client authenticates and gets an IP.

screens.title: WPA2‑Personal (PSK) Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: WPA2‑Personal uses a pre‑shared key to authenticate all clients to a WLAN. It is simple to deploy and appropriate for small sites or labs where managing individual credentials is impractical. The key decision is the strength and management of the passphrase: use a long, complex key and change it periodically. In the WLC you select WPA2 policy, enable AES (CCMP), and set the PSK. I’ll walk through a short CLI example which enables WPA2, turns on AES ciphers, and sets an ASCII pre‑shared key. After you configure the PSK, map the WLAN to the correct dynamic interface so clients obtain the expected IP addresses. A common mistake is reusing a simple passphrase or never rotating it; this reduces security. Another misconception is that PSK provides individual accountability — it does not. For accountability and per‑user keys, you would use WPA2‑Enterprise with 802.1X and RADIUS. Key takeaway: WPA2‑PSK is fast to deploy, but reserve it for small or controlled environments and manage keys responsibly. Try connecting a test client after configuration and verify it receives an IP from the mapped VLAN.

keyIdea.title: PSK Tradeoffs
keyIdea.text: WPA2-PSK is easy and quick, but lacks per-user authentication; use strong, rotated passphrases and reserve PSK for small deployments.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › WPA2‑Personal (PSK)
When to use PSK
Ideal for small deployments, test environments, or guest networks when individualized credentials are not necessary.
Best practices
  • Use a long, complex passphrase and rotate it regularly.
  • Limit PSK use to environments where shared credentials are acceptable.
  • Monitor client lists and change PSK if a compromise is suspected.
Misconception
PSK does not provide per-user accountability; all users share the same credential.
Key Takeaway

PSK is quick and easy, but for enterprise authentication and accountability, use 802.1X with RADIUS.

CLI Walkthrough
! Configure WPA2-Personal (PSK) for WLAN ID 2
(WLC)> config wlan security wpa wpa2 enable 2
(WLC)> config wlan security wpa wpa2 ciphers aes enable 2
(WLC)> config wlan security wpa wpa2 psk set-key ascii CohortiaWLAN!23 2
Verification
After configuration, connect a client with the configured passphrase and check it receives an IP from the WLAN’s mapped VLAN.

screens.title: WPA2‑Enterprise (802.1X) — Conceptual Overview
screens.narratorSegment: WPA2‑Enterprise uses 802.1X with a RADIUS server to authenticate each user or device individually. Unlike PSK, which shares a single pre‑shared key among all clients, 802.1X issues dynamic keys per session and integrates with centralized identity stores. Conceptually, when a client attempts to join, the WLC forwards the authentication request to a configured RADIUS server that validates credentials and then allows or denies access. This method provides per-user accountability, scalable credential management, and stronger security. A concrete example: an employee enters corporate username and password; the RADIUS server validates them and the WLC applies the WLAN policy with AES encryption. A misconception is that 802.1X is always more complex to manage; it does require infrastructure (a RADIUS server) and certificate management, but the operational benefits in an enterprise — such as revoking a single user’s access — outweigh the setup cost. Key takeaway: use 802.1X for enterprise-grade authentication and PSK only when centralized authentication is impractical. Which user policies would you enforce via RADIUS roles in your deployment? WPA2‑Enterprise (802.1X) — Conceptual Overview means 802.1x with radius authenticates each user individually, providing dynamic keys and accountability needed in enterprise environments.. In practical terms, why enterprises use 802.1x and how it differs from psk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: 802.1X with RADIUS authenticates each user individually, providing dynamic keys and accountability needed in enterprise environments.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › WPA2‑Enterprise Overview
Side-by-side: PSK vs 802.1X
WPA2‑Personal (PSK)
Shared pre‑shared key, simple deployment, no per-user accountability, best for small sites.
WPA2‑Enterprise (802.1X)
Uses RADIUS, provides per-user authentication, dynamic session keys, and enterprise policy enforcement.
Concrete Scenario
An employee authenticates with corporate credentials. RADIUS validates the user and the WLC grants access with AES encryption and a dynamically negotiated key.
Operational considerations
  • Requires a RADIUS server and certificates for strong mutual authentication.
  • Enables role-based policies and easier revocation of individual access.
  • More setup overhead but provides superior security for enterprises.
Pro Tip
Start by testing 802.1X in a lab with a single RADIUS entry to gain familiarity before rolling out widely.

screens.title: VLAN Mapping and Dynamic Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: VLAN mapping on the WLC associates a WLAN — the SSID and its security policy — with a logical interface called a dynamic interface. That dynamic interface represents a VLAN and carries the client traffic into the wired network and to the correct DHCP scope. Without that mapping, clients may connect to the SSID but not receive the expected IP address. In practice you create or confirm the dynamic interface on the WLC, assign it an IP address in the VLAN’s subnet, and then map the WLAN to that interface. For example, map the Corporate SSID to interface vlan10 so clients receive addresses from 192.168.10.0/24. A common troubleshooting misstep is assuming the wired switch VLAN configuration alone is enough: the WLC must also have the dynamic interface defined and correctly mapped. Key takeaway: VLAN mapping is the bridge between wireless SSIDs and wired network segmentation. When verifying, check the WLC Interfaces page, confirm the interface IP, and ensure the switch ports carry the correct VLAN as a trunk to the WLC path. VLAN Mapping and Dynamic Interfaces means assign each wlan to a dynamic interface representing a vlan so client traffic enters the correct subnet and receives dhcp.. In practical terms, how ssids are associated with vlans on the wlc. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Assign each WLAN to a dynamic interface representing a VLAN so client traffic enters the correct subnet and receives DHCP.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › VLAN Mapping & Dynamic Interfaces
Concept
A dynamic interface on the WLC represents a VLAN. Map each WLAN to the proper dynamic interface so client traffic is segmented correctly.
Checklist to map a WLAN
  1. Create or verify the dynamic interface on the WLC and give it an IP in the VLAN subnet.
  2. Map the WLAN to that dynamic interface in the WLAN settings.
  3. Ensure the upstream switch port is trunking the VLAN to the WLC or APs as required.
  4. Test DHCP assignment from a client connected to the SSID.
Common Mistake
Assuming the wired VLAN exists on switches is enough. The WLC must also host or route the dynamic interface for the WLAN mapping to work.
Example mapping
Map SSID Corporate to WLAN ID 1 and interface vlan10 with gateway 192.168.10.1 so clients get addresses from the 192.168.10.0/24 pool.
Verification steps
  • On the WLC, check Interfaces to confirm vlan10 exists and its IP.
  • Ensure the WLAN is mapped to vlan10 in WLAN settings.
  • From a client, confirm DHCP assignment and ping gateway in that VLAN.
Why it matters

Correct VLAN mapping prevents clients from joining an SSID but remaining isolated without IP services.

screens.title: AP Discovery and CAPWAP Association
screens.narratorSegment: In controller-based wireless, Access Points operate as lightweight devices that rely on the controller for configuration. When an AP boots it attempts to discover a WLC by several methods: DHCP option 43, DNS entry, or a locally configured WLC IP. Once it discovers the controller it establishes a CAPWAP tunnel — Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points — to exchange control messages and receive the configuration such as SSIDs, channels and power settings. CAPWAP uses specific UDP ports and if firewalls block those ports, APs cannot join. A concrete troubleshooting example: an AP cannot join; check whether DHCP option 43 is set, confirm DNS resolves the controller name, verify network connectivity, and ensure UDP 5246/5247 are open. A common misconception is that APs will function fully without a controller in lightweight mode; they will not broadcast centrally managed SSIDs or obtain policy without a successful CAPWAP association. Key takeaway: AP discovery and CAPWAP connectivity are prerequisites for broadcasting controller-managed WLANs. How would you validate CAPWAP status on the WLC when an AP fails to appear? AP Discovery and CAPWAP Association means aps discover wlcs via dhcp option 43, dns, or local ip and then form capwap tunnels to receive configuration.. In practical terms, how lightweight aps find and join the wlc. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: In controller-based wireless, Access Points operate as lightweight devices that rely on the controller for configuration. When an AP boots it attempts to discover a WLC by several methods: DHCP option 43, DNS entry, or a locally configured WLC IP. Once it discovers the controller it establishes a CAPWAP tunnel — Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points — to exchange control messages and receive the configuration such as SSIDs, channels and power settings. CAPWAP uses specific UDP ports and if firewalls block those ports, APs cannot join. A concrete troubleshooting example: an AP cannot join; check whether DHCP option 43 is set, confirm DNS resolves the controller name, verify network connectivity, and ensure UDP 5246/5247 are open. A common misconception is that APs will function fully without a controller in lightweight mode; they will not broadcast centrally managed SSIDs or obtain policy without a successful CAPWAP association. Key takeaway: AP discovery and CAPWAP connectivity are prerequisites for broadcasting controller-managed WLANs. How would you validate CAPWAP status on the WLC when an AP fails to appear? AP Discovery and CAPWAP Association means aps discover wlcs via dhcp option 43, dns, or local ip and then form capwap tunnels to receive configuration.. In practical terms, how lightweight aps find and join the wlc. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: AP Discovery & CAPWAP

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › AP Discovery & CAPWAP
Discovery Methods
APs use DHCP option 43, DNS, or a locally-stored WLC IP to find the controller before forming CAPWAP.
DHCP Option 43
Configured on the DHCP server to point APs to the WLC IP for automatic discovery.
DNS
APs can resolve a predefined controller hostname via DNS to locate the WLC.
Local IP
APs can have a stored WLC IP to use when DHCP or DNS discovery are not available.
CAPWAP Basics
CAPWAP establishes control and data plane tunnels so the controller can push SSID configurations and collect status from APs.
Troubleshooting checklist
  • Confirm AP can reach WLC IP and that UDP 5246 and 5247 are not blocked.
  • Verify DHCP option 43 or DNS entries are correctly configured.
  • On the WLC, check the Access Points page for join attempts and error messages.
Key Takeaway

Without successful discovery and CAPWAP, APs will not receive SSID configs and cannot serve controller-managed WLANs.

screens.title: Verifying WLAN Operation
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is the step that confirms your configuration works for end users. On the WLC you can observe connected clients, their signal strength, association state, and data rates. From a client perspective, the basic checks are: connect to the SSID, confirm DHCP assigns an IP, and verify access to internal or internet resources. If a client fails to get an IP, check the mapped dynamic interface exists on the WLC and that DHCP servers are reachable on that VLAN. Performance problems often manifest as low data rates or frequent disconnects; inspect RSSI values and channel overlap. A concrete example: a client connects to MyCorpNet but cannot reach any resource — you would validate the WLAN mapping to vlan20, confirm the WLC’s vlan20 interface IP, verify the switch trunk carries vlan20, and ensure the DHCP server is serving that subnet. A common mistake is checking only the client device; include WLC logs and AP load statistics to see shared causes. Key takeaway: combine client-level checks with controller and AP telemetry to quickly isolate configuration versus RF or wired issues. Verifying WLAN Operation means verify both client dhcp/ip and wlc/ap telemetry (rssi, data rate, client list) to find configuration or rf issues.. Top: Key Verification Steps
Client IP
Confirm DHCP assigns an address in the VLAN mapped to the SSID.
WLC Client List
Check client association, RSSI, and data rate on the controller.
AP Load
Inspect APs for high client density or resource constraints that affect throughput.
Bottom: Example Verification Workflow
Client steps

  2. Confirm IP via DHCP and default gateway reachability.
  3. Ping internal resources or internet to verify data path.
Controller checks

screens.title: Common Wireless Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting wireless requires a logical order and both wireless and wired checks. Start with the client: ensure the correct SSID, passphrase, and that the wireless adapter is enabled. If the client fails to authenticate, compare the configured WPA version and cipher on the WLC to the client settings. When clients connect but lack IP addresses, suspect VLAN mapping or DHCP reachability: verify the dynamic interface exists on the WLC and that the DHCP server serves that VLAN. For AP not joining the controller, check network connectivity, verify DHCP option 43 or DNS discovery is configured, and ensure UDP ports 5246 and 5247 are allowed. For poor performance, check RSSI, channel overlap, and client density — RF planning or channel reassignments may be required. A concrete example: guests on GuestWiFi not receiving IPs often trace back to the Guest WLAN not being mapped to its vlan50 interface on the WLC. Common misconception: rebooting APs fixes persistent RF or policy issues; reboot may help transient faults, but misconfiguration and planning issues require systematic checks. Key takeaway: follow client → AP → controller → network sequence and document observed behavior at each step to isolate the cause.

Stepwise Troubleshooting Flow
  1. Client: SSID, credentials, adapter state.
  2. Authentication: WPA version and cipher mismatch checks.
  3. DHCP/IP: Verify WLC VLAN mapping and DHCP server reachability.
  4. AP: Confirm discovery method and CAPWAP connectivity; check UDP 5246/5247.

Example Issue
GuestWiFi clients not getting IPs — check that GuestWiFi is mapped to dynamic interface vlan50 and that DHCP for vlan50 is reachable.

Log findings step-by-step and avoid repeated reboots; document the fault signs to speed root cause identification.

screens.title: RF Planning Essentials
screens.narratorSegment: RF planning is the design practice that prevents coverage holes and capacity shortfalls. Good planning considers coverage (signal reaches user areas), capacity (APs support expected client counts), and interference (minimize co‑channel overlap). In an enterprise, perform a site survey or a predictive design to determine AP placement and channel plans. A simple predictive design can prevent common errors such as placing too few APs in high-density areas or clustering AP channels leading to interference. Concrete example: a conference room expecting 50 clients needs higher AP density and careful channel planning compared to a small office. A common misconception is that more APs always improve performance; in fact, too many overlapping APs on the same channel increase contention and reduce throughput. Key takeaway: balance coverage and capacity, plan channels to reduce overlap, and validate with walk tests or analyzers. In lab work, adjust AP transmit power and channels based on observed signal and interference rather than default autopilot settings. RF Planning Essentials means design ap placement for both coverage and capacity; avoid channel overlap and tune power settings after validation.. In practical terms, coverage, capacity, interference, and placement best practices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Key factors
  • Coverage: ensure signal strength reaches intended user locations.
  • Capacity: design for number of simultaneous users per area.
  • Interference: plan non-overlapping channels and avoid co-channel saturation.
Practical checks
Run a predictive survey or a site walk test, tune AP transmit power, and adjust channels based on observed noise and client experience.
Common mistakes
  • Relying solely on default AP settings without validation.
  • Adding APs to boost signal without reconsidering channel plan.
  • Neglecting client density when choosing AP count and location.
Key Takeaway

RF planning is essential for predictable wireless performance; validate designs with surveys and adjust settings based on measurements.

screens.title: Simulated Lab: Configure an Employee WLAN
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough guides you through configuring a basic WLAN on a simulated WLC. Begin in the WLC CLI or GUI and create a new WLAN with ID 2 and SSID MyCorpNet. Add a clear description such as Employee Network and enable the WLAN. Next, configure WPA2 policy, enable AES ciphers, and set the ASCII pre‑shared key CohortiaWLAN!23. Finally map the WLAN to the dynamic interface vlan20 which must exist on the WLC and correspond to the 192.168.20.0/24 subnet. After these steps, connect a test client using the passphrase and verify it gets an IP from 192.168.20. x. A common misstep is assuming the VLAN exists on the wired network automatically; you must ensure both the WLC and network switch agree on VLAN configuration. Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Simulated Lab: Employee WLAN
Lab Instructions
  1. Create WLAN: Profile Name Employee_WLAN, SSID MyCorpNet, WLAN ID 2.
  2. Enable the WLAN and add a description "Employee Network".
  3. Configure security: WPA2, Authentication PSK, Cipher AES, PSK CohortiaWLAN!23.
  4. Map WLAN ID 2 to dynamic interface vlan20 (assume vlan20 exists with IP 192.168.20.1/24).
  5. Verify with a client: join SSID with PSK and confirm IP from 192.168.20.0/24.

Simulated CLI Commands
! Create a new WLAN (SSID)
(WLC)> config wlan create 2 MyCorpNet MyCorpNet
(WLC)> config wlan description 2 "Employee Network"
(WLC)> config wlan enable 2

! Configure WPA2-Personal (PSK) security for WLAN ID 2
(WLC)> config wlan security wpa wpa2 enable 2
(WLC)> config wlan security wpa wpa2 ciphers aes enable 2
(WLC)> config wlan security wpa wpa2 psk set-key ascii CohortiaWLAN!23 2

! Map WLAN ID 2 to dynamic interface vlan20
(WLC)> config wlan interface 2 vlan20

! Verify configuration
(WLC)> show wlan 2
Key Takeaway

Follow create, secure, map, and verify. Document each step so you can quickly revert or replicate the configuration.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: These three concise concepts capture the essentials you should remember. First, the Wireless LAN Controller is the central point for managing multiple lightweight APs; configure and secure its management interface before deploying WLANs. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how a Wireless LAN Controller becomes the centralized point for enterprise Wi‑Fi, why SSIDs map to VLANs, how lightweight Access Points discover and join a controller, and the practical steps to secure and verify a WLAN. We begin with the realistic initial setup tasks: assigning a management IP, setting DNS and gateway, and creating strong administrative credentials. Then you will see how SSIDs are created on the controller, how security options differ between WPA2-Personal and WPA2-Enterprise, and why VLAN mapping isolates traffic. You will also learn the AP discovery methods and how CAPWAP tunnels carry configuration from controller to AP. Finally, we cover verification checks and common troubleshooting patterns such as client not receiving DHCP, AP failing to register, and poor RF planning. Each topic includes a concrete CLI or GUI example and a hands-on scenario to practice. By the end of these screens you should be able to perform a basic WLC configuration, create a secure SSID mapped to a VLAN, confirm AP association, and run the first checks when a wireless client experiences issues. Consider how you would confirm a client’s VLAN and signal strength during troubleshooting.

These objectives frame practical competence with controller-based wireless. First, you will perform an initial WLC setup: assigning a management IP, configuring DNS and gateway, and creating secure administrative credentials. This matters because an accessible, well-protected management plane is the foundation for every subsequent WLAN configuration. Second, you will configure SSIDs on the WLC and map them to VLANs. Creating SSIDs and mapping them to logical interfaces separates traffic like corporate and guest networks and ensures clients receive addresses from the right DHCP pool. Third, you will associate APs to a WLC and understand discovery methods and the CAPWAP tunnel. Knowing how APs find and join the controller helps you diagnose join failures and ensure APs receive the correct configuration. Fourth, you will implement WPA2-Personal and conceptually understand WPA2-Enterprise with a RADIUS server, and verify WLAN operation. Proper security and verification prevent unauthorized access and ensure clients can reach network resources. Each objective links to hands-on checks and common troubleshooting steps so you can both configure and validate your wireless deployment.

This second objectives slide gives you a practical checklist you can follow in a lab. Start by securing the WLC management plane: set a management IP, configure DNS and gateway, and change default admin credentials. Doing this prevents unauthorized controller configuration. Next, create WLAN profiles and SSIDs, and choose the correct encryption. For small deployments, WPA2-Personal with AES suffices; for enterprises, configure WPA2-Enterprise with a RADIUS server. Each WLAN must be mapped to a dynamic interface — a logical representation of a VLAN on the WLC — so clients receive IP addresses from the correct subnet. Then, ensure APs can discover the controller using DHCP option 43, DNS, or a locally stored IP and that CAPWAP is allowed through firewalls. Finally, practice verification: join a client, check DHCP assignment, inspect client RSSI and data rate, and review AP join status on the WLC. These steps form a reproducible workflow for lab and real deployments.

Initial setup of a Wireless LAN Controller is the moment you establish control, security, and reachability for your wireless domain. A WLC needs a management IP, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS so administrators can access it from the network. You will also create administrative credentials. These basic settings are not optional: if the management IP is incorrect or the gateway is missing, APs and administrators may not reach the controller. Configure DNS so the WLC can resolve names during some discovery workflows. Immediately change default passwords and restrict which management hosts can access the controller to reduce risk. A concrete example: assign the WLC management interface 192.168.1.10/24 with gateway 192.168.1.1 and DNS 192.168.1.2, then create an admin account with a strong passphrase. A common misconception is that APs can always register without the management plane secured — they may join technically, but unsecured management credentials leave the whole deployment vulnerable. Key takeaway: the management plane is the root of trust for controller-based Wi‑Fi. Verify connectivity with a browser to the default management IP or a console session and confirm you can reach the WLC from your management workstation. What access controls will you put in place for your controller?

Creating a WLAN on a WLC means defining a profile the controller uses to broadcast an SSID to clients and to apply security and network mapping. The process begins by choosing a profile name for internal reference and an SSID that users will see. You then enable the WLAN and select security settings. For example, choose the WPA2 policy and enable AES to use CCMP encryption. In the controller GUI the path is typically WLANs → Create New; in the CLI you create the WLAN ID, give it a name, enable it, and attach security settings. An example CLI sequence creates WLAN ID 2 with SSID MyCorpNet, enables it, configures WPA2-PSK and AES, and maps it to a VLAN interface named vlan20. A common misconception is that SSID broadcasting alone controls access; in reality, security policy and VLAN mapping determine authentication and network reachability. Key takeaway: a WLAN is a bundle of SSID, security policy, and network interface mapping — all three must be correct for users to connect and get an IP on the intended subnet. How would you document your WLAN naming and VLAN strategy for a multi-SSID deployment?

WPA2‑Personal uses a pre‑shared key to authenticate all clients to a WLAN. It is simple to deploy and appropriate for small sites or labs where managing individual credentials is impractical. The key decision is the strength and management of the passphrase: use a long, complex key and change it periodically. In the WLC you select WPA2 policy, enable AES (CCMP), and set the PSK. I’ll walk through a short CLI example which enables WPA2, turns on AES ciphers, and sets an ASCII pre‑shared key. After you configure the PSK, map the WLAN to the correct dynamic interface so clients obtain the expected IP addresses. A common mistake is reusing a simple passphrase or never rotating it; this reduces security. Another misconception is that PSK provides individual accountability — it does not. For accountability and per‑user keys, you would use WPA2‑Enterprise with 802.1X and RADIUS. Key takeaway: WPA2‑PSK is fast to deploy, but reserve it for small or controlled environments and manage keys responsibly. Try connecting a test client after configuration and verify it receives an IP from the mapped VLAN.

WPA2‑Enterprise uses 802.1X with a RADIUS server to authenticate each user or device individually. Unlike PSK, which shares a single pre‑shared key among all clients, 802.1X issues dynamic keys per session and integrates with centralized identity stores. Conceptually, when a client attempts to join, the WLC forwards the authentication request to a configured RADIUS server that validates credentials and then allows or denies access. This method provides per-user accountability, scalable credential management, and stronger security. A concrete example: an employee enters corporate username and password; the RADIUS server validates them and the WLC applies the WLAN policy with AES encryption. VLAN mapping on the WLC associates a WLAN — the SSID and its security policy — with a logical interface called a dynamic interface. That dynamic interface represents a VLAN and carries the client traffic into the wired network and to the correct DHCP scope. Without that mapping, clients may connect to the SSID but not receive the expected IP address. In practice you create or confirm the dynamic interface on the WLC, assign it an IP address in the VLAN’s subnet, and then map the WLAN to that interface. For example, map the Corporate SSID to interface vlan10 so clients receive addresses from 192.168.10.0/24. A common troubleshooting misstep is assuming the wired switch VLAN configuration alone is enough: the WLC must also have the dynamic interface defined and correctly mapped. Key takeaway: VLAN mapping is the bridge between wireless SSIDs and wired network segmentation. In controller-based wireless, Access Points operate as lightweight devices that rely on the controller for configuration. When an AP boots it attempts to discover a WLC by several methods: DHCP option 43, DNS entry, or a locally configured WLC IP. Once it discovers the controller it establishes a CAPWAP tunnel — Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points — to exchange control messages and receive the configuration such as SSIDs, channels and power settings. CAPWAP uses specific UDP ports and if firewalls block those ports, APs cannot join. A concrete troubleshooting example: an AP cannot join; check whether DHCP option 43 is set, confirm DNS resolves the controller name, verify network connectivity, and ensure UDP 5246/5247 are open. A common misconception is that APs will function fully without a controller in lightweight mode; they will not broadcast centrally managed SSIDs or obtain policy without a successful CAPWAP association. If a client fails to get an IP, check the mapped dynamic interface exists on the WLC and that DHCP servers are reachable on that VLAN. Troubleshooting wireless requires a logical order and both wireless and wired checks. Start with the client: ensure the correct SSID, passphrase, and that the wireless adapter is enabled. If the client fails to authenticate, compare the configured WPA version and cipher on the WLC to the client settings. When clients connect but lack IP addresses, suspect VLAN mapping or DHCP reachability: verify the dynamic interface exists on the WLC and that the DHCP server serves that VLAN. For AP not joining the controller, check network connectivity, verify DHCP option 43 or DNS discovery is configured, and ensure UDP ports 5246 and 5247 are allowed. For poor performance, check RSSI, channel overlap, and client density — RF planning or channel reassignments may be required. A concrete example: guests on GuestWiFi not receiving IPs often trace back to the Guest WLAN not being mapped to its vlan50 interface on the WLC. Common misconception: rebooting APs fixes persistent RF or policy issues; reboot may help transient faults, but misconfiguration and planning issues require systematic checks. Key takeaway: follow client → AP → controller → network sequence and document observed behavior at each step to isolate the cause.

RF planning is the design practice that prevents coverage holes and capacity shortfalls. Good planning considers coverage (signal reaches user areas), capacity (APs support expected client counts), and interference (minimize co‑channel overlap). In an enterprise, perform a site survey or a predictive design to determine AP placement and channel plans. A simple predictive design can prevent common errors such as placing too few APs in high-density areas or clustering AP channels leading to interference. Concrete example: a conference room expecting 50 clients needs higher AP density and careful channel planning compared to a small office. A common misconception is that more APs always improve performance; in fact, too many overlapping APs on the same channel increase contention and reduce throughput. Key takeaway: balance coverage and capacity, plan channels to reduce overlap, and validate with walk tests or analyzers. In lab work, adjust AP transmit power and channels based on observed signal and interference rather than default autopilot settings. These three concise concepts capture the essentials you should remember. First, the Wireless LAN Controller is the central point for managing multiple lightweight APs; configure and secure its management interface before deploying WLANs. Second, a WLAN is a bundle: SSID, security policy, and a mapped dynamic interface that represents a VLAN. All three must be correct for clients to authenticate and receive an IP from the intended subnet. Third, AP discovery and CAPWAP association are required for APs to receive configuration; verify discovery methods and ensure CAPWAP ports are permitted. Keep these three ideas in mind when you design, deploy, and troubleshoot a controller‑based wireless network.
